overrides.after: How long did the money grow to become twice as large? A logarithm finds the missing input of an exponential. But what if the input also records turns, and several different numbers lead to the same point? Then undoing the exponential needs a choice. And when numbers become matrices, even the question ‘can it be undone?’ gets subtler.

overrides.after: The real exponential rises continuously from values near zero to arbitrarily large values. It never reaches zero, and it never visits a negative output. So every positive real number has exactly one real input: its natural logarithm. The logarithm of one is zero. The logarithm of e is one. The logarithm of zero is not a real number, nor is the real logarithm of a negative number.

overrides.after: To make one continuous choice, we restrict where we allow ourselves to travel. A common choice removes the nonpositive real axis and uses angles strictly between minus pi and pi. On that slit plane, the principal logarithm is a single analytic function. The cut marks where our chosen angle would jump; it is a choice of domain, not a crack in space.

overrides.after: Even after choosing a branch, log of a product need not equal the sum of the chosen logs. If two angles are each three quarters of pi, their sum is one and a half pi.
